edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina 5 (1844), via Latin Wikisource
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Militiae nomen cum dederis, freno teneris. Incipe tunc ergo dimittere pristina gesta: Luxurias vita, quoniam labor imminet armis. Imperio regis omni virtute parendum, Tempora postrema si vis pertingere laeta. Ille bonus miles, semper exspecta fruenda; Blandire noli tibi, desidias omnino mitte, Ut tuo praeposito cottidie praesto sis, ante Solicitus esto, matutinus signa revise. Cum videris bellum, agonia sume propinqua. Haec gloria regis, militem videre paratum; Rex adest, optato propter spem dominicaturum. Ille parat dona, ille pro victoria laetus Suspicit, et proprium satellem dedicat esse. Tu tibi praeterea in Belian parcere noli: Impiger esto magis, ut reddat famam pro morte.
pass_a_gloss: When you have given the name of soldier, you are held by a bridle. Begin then to dismiss former deeds: a life of luxury, because labor with arms is imminent. To the command of the King, obedience is to be given with all virtue, if you wish to reach the last times happily. He is a good soldier, who always expects things to be enjoyed; do not flatter yourself, completely dismiss idleness, so that you may be present daily to your commander, be solicitous beforehand, revise the signs in the morning. When you see war, take up nearby agony. This is the glory of the King, to see the soldier prepared; the King is present, who will dominate because of hope. He prepares gifts, he is joyful for victory, looks up at the situation, and dedicates his own attendant to be. Do not spare yourself besides in Belial: be more energetic, so that he may give fame as a reward for death.

pass_b_english: Once you take the name of soldier, a bridle holds you fast. So begin now to cast off your former deeds: a life of luxury, because armed labor is at hand. You must obey the King's command with every virtue, if you wish to reach the last times happily. A good soldier always awaits the rewards to come; do not coddle yourself, root out all idleness, so that you may stand ready each day before your commander. Be watchful beforehand; review the signals at dawn. When you see war, take up the agony close at hand. This is the King's glory: to see his soldier prepared. The King is present, who will reign because of the hoped-for hope. He prepares gifts; he rejoices in victory, looks up at the field, and appoints his own attendant to serve. Do not spare yourself in Belial besides; be all the more vigorous, so that he may grant you renown as the reward for death.

review.notes: Pass B contains a redundancy/error in translating 'optato propter spem' as 'because of the hoped-for hope', which contradicts the lemma choice and the Latin 'spem' (hope). Pass A contains a significant mistranslation of 'Suspicit, et proprium satellem dedicat esse' as 'looks up at the situation, and dedicates his own attendant to be', which is ungrammatical and fails to capture the sense of the Latin (likely 'he looks up/observes and appoints his own attendant').
uncertainties: The phrase 'dedicat esse' in 'proprium satellem dedicat esse' is syntactically awkward in the Latin and leads to the broken English in Pass A ('dedicates his own attendant to be').
reasons: Pass B translates 'optato propter spem' as 'because of the hoped-for hope', which is a tautology not present in the Latin 'optato propter spem'.
Pass A translates 'dedicat esse' as 'dedicates his own attendant to be', which is a failure of fidelity to sense/grammar.
